questions.title: Passage 1: The Elderly Carpenter and the House
questions.passage:
An elderly carpenter was ready to retire. He told his employer of his plans to leave the house building business and live a more leisurely life with his family. He would miss the pay cheque, but he needed to retire. The employer was sorry to see his good worker go and asked if he could build just one more house as a personal favour. The carpenter said ‘yes’, but in time it was easy to see that his heart was not in his work. He resorted to shoddy workmanship and used inferior material. It was an unfortunate way to end his career. When the carpenter finished his work, his employer handed over the key of the house to the carpenter— “This is your house, my gift to you.”

What a shock! What a shame! If he had only known he was building his own house, he would have done it all so differently! Now he had to live in a poorly built house. So it is with us. We build our lives, a day at a time, often putting less than our best into the building. Then, with a shock, we realize we have to live in the house we have built. If we could do it over, we would do it much differently. But, you cannot go back. You are the carpenter, and every day you hammer a nail, place a board, or erect a wall. Someone once said, your attitude, and the choices you make today, help build the “house” you will live in tomorrow. Therefore, build wisely!

The carpenter stood before his shoddy creation, the heavy key weighing down his hand like a block of lead. He looked at the crooked doors and the weak foundation, weeping for the craftsmanship and integrity he had thrown away out of sheer impatience. He realized that the only way to find peace was to spend his retirement years rebuilding the structure, replacing every cheap board with strong oak, ensuring his legacy ended with pride rather than regret.

Like that old man. We often forget that the foundation we lay today determines the shelter we enjoy tomorrow. Every kind word spoken, every honest hour worked and every difficult choice made with integrity is a sturdy beam in the architecture of our character. Do not wait for the final keys to be handed over to regret the shortcuts you took; build with your finest efforts right now, for you must live in the house of your own making.

subparts.question: Does the elderly carpenter build the final house poorly using subpar materials?
options: (i) He was angry at his employer for forcing him to work during his twilight years.
(ii) He was eager to retire and did not put his full effort and care into the project.
(iii) He was running out of the funds provided by his employer to buy good quality materials.
(iv) He had lost his carpentry skills and knowledge due to his old age.
subparts.answer: (ii) He was eager to retire and did not put his full effort and care into the project.
subparts.explanation: The passage states that the carpenter agreed to build one last house as a personal favour, but 'in time it was easy to see that his heart was not in his work. He resorted to shoddy workmanship and used inferior material' because he was ready to retire and live a leisurely life.

subparts.question: What surprise does the employer reveal to the carpenter after the house is completely built?
options: (i) He asks the carpenter to tear it down and build a better one.
(ii) He deducts money from the carpenter's pension to pay for the damages.
(iii) He fires the carpenter for his poor workmanship on the project.
(iv) He gives the keys of the house to the carpenter as a retirement gift.
subparts.answer: (iv) He gives the keys of the house to the carpenter as a retirement gift.
subparts.explanation: When the carpenter finished his work, the employer handed over the key and said, 'This is your house, my gift to you.'

subparts.question: What is the antonym of "shoddy"?
options: (i) Inferior
(ii) Trashy
(iii) Superior
(iv) Mediocre
subparts.answer: (iii) Superior
subparts.explanation: 'Shoddy' means badly made or of poor quality. 'Superior' means higher in quality or excellence, which is its direct opposite (antonym).

subparts.question: When the carpenter realizes the house is for him, he feels embarrassed. What does this realization symbolize?
options: (i) The importance of always asking for help on large projects.
(ii) The need to change professions when one gets older.
(iii) The realization that we must live with the consequences of the choices we make today.
(iv) The regret of not earning more money during his career.
subparts.answer: (iii) The realization that we must live with the consequences of the choices we make today.
subparts.explanation: The author draws a parallel between the carpenter's house and our lives: the choices, shortcuts, and attitudes we adopt each day construct the future consequences we ultimately must live with.

subparts.question: Which of the following best states the primary moral lesson of the story?
options: (i) Always prioritize quantity over quality when you are ready to retire.
(ii) Always do your best and act with integrity, because you are ultimately building your own future.
(iii) Trust your employer to reward you fairly for all your efforts.
(iv) Retirement is the most important goal in a person's life.
subparts.answer: (ii) Always do your best and act with integrity, because you are ultimately building your own future.
subparts.explanation: The moral of the passage is encapsulated in the concluding lines: build with your finest efforts and integrity right now, because each person must live in the house (life and character) of their own making.

subparts.question: What did the carpenter tell his employer?
subparts.answer: The carpenter told his employer about his plans to retire from the house-building business and live a more leisurely life with his family.
subparts.explanation: Found in the first two sentences of paragraph 1.

subparts.question: What favour did his employer ask from the carpenter?
subparts.answer: The employer asked the carpenter if he could build just one more house as a personal favour before leaving his job.
subparts.explanation: Found in paragraph 1: 'The employer was sorry to see his good worker go and asked if he could build just one more house as a personal favour.'

subparts.question: What specific type of wood did the carpenter plan to use to replace the cheap boards during his retirement?
subparts.answer: The carpenter planned to use strong oak to replace every cheap board.
subparts.explanation: Found in paragraph 3: 'replacing every cheap board with strong oak, ensuring his legacy ended with pride rather than regret.'

subparts.question: According to the text, what two things do we choose or possess today that directly help build the "house" we live in tomorrow?
subparts.answer: Our attitude and the choices we make today directly help build the "house" we live in tomorrow.
subparts.explanation: Paragraph 2 explicitly states: 'Someone once said, your attitude, and the choices you make today, help build the “house” you will live in tomorrow.'

subparts.question: Which word in the first paragraph means the same as 'art of skill of a workman'?
subparts.answer: Workmanship
subparts.explanation: Paragraph 1 states: 'He resorted to shoddy workmanship...'. 'Workmanship' denotes the degree of skill or art with which an object or product is made by a craftsman.

questions.title: Passage 2: Australia’s 2019-2020 Bushfire Season Was Not Normal
questions.passage:
Australia’s 2019-2020 Bushfire Season was not Normal

1. Data from satellite sources assembled by the United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) World Environment Situation Room confirms that the wildfires in Australia in the last two months of 2019 and the first six weeks of 2020 were far from normal. 2019 was the second hottest year on record since 1880, and Australia recorded its warmest temperatures ever in December 2019.

2. “Rising temperatures continue to melt records. The past decade was the hottest on record. Scientists tell us that ocean temperatures are now rising at the equivalent of five Hiroshima bombs a second. One million species are in near-term danger of extinction. Our planet is burning,” says United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres.

3. “The trend is very clear: 37 of the last 40 years were the warmest recorded since 1880, and the six warmest years recorded were the last six years,” says Pascal Peduzzi, Director of UNEP’s Global Resource Information Database in Geneva. “For those who think Australia is always burning, graphs clearly show that these fires were exceptional.”

4. “This service, accessible via the UNEP’s World Environment Situation Room, is provided for all countries at national and provincial levels. It identifies trends in wildfire activity since 2003, when the data first became available and monitoring began. We have sliced and diced the satellite-based data on wildfires worldwide from 2009 to the present day. We analyse the wildfires’ data by month, type of land cover, protected area, province and nation to produce information products,” Peduzzi adds. (Source: UN Environment)

5. The ecological toll of these blazes extends far beyond the immediate charred landscape, as massive smoke plumes inject millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide into the stratosphere, creating a dangerous feedback loop. UN experts emphasize that mitigating such unprecedented disasters requires immediate, coordinated global action, including transitioning away from fossil fuels and investing in tech-driven early warning systems.

6. Furthermore, the destruction of critical habitats has pushed fragile ecosystems to the brink, forcing conservationists to rethink long-term biodiversity preservation strategies. As communities rebuild among the ashes, UNEP highlights the urgent need to integrate traditional Indigenous land management techniques with modern satellite data to foster climate resilience.

subparts.question: What do the reports confirm about the 2019-20 Australian fires?
options: (i) the fires were not normal
(ii) the fires were normal
(iii) the fires were natural
(iv) data inconclusive
subparts.answer: (i) the fires were not normal
subparts.explanation: Paragraph 1 clearly states that UNEP satellite data confirms the wildfires 'were far from normal'.

subparts.question: What was the difference in the recorded temperatures in 2019 from the 1880s?
options: (i) 2019 recorded the wettest temperatures since 1880s
(ii) 2019 recorded the hottest temperatures ever
(iii) 2019 recorded the cooler temperatures than 1880s
(iv) 2019 recorded the warmest temperatures since 1880s
subparts.answer: (iv) 2019 recorded the warmest temperatures since 1880s
subparts.explanation: Paragraph 1 states: '2019 was the second hottest year on record since 1880, and Australia recorded its warmest temperatures ever in December 2019.' Thus 2019 recorded the warmest temperatures since 1880s.

subparts.question: What comparison has been made between the rising sea temperatures and Hiroshima?
options: (i) ocean temperatures are rising at the equivalent of three Hiroshima bombs a second
(ii) ocean temperatures are rising at the equivalent of five Hiroshima bombs a second
(iii) ocean temperatures are rising at the equivalent of five Hiroshima bombs an hour
(iv) none of these
subparts.answer: (ii) ocean temperatures are rising at the equivalent of five Hiroshima bombs a second
subparts.explanation: Paragraph 2 quotes António Guterres: 'Scientists tell us that ocean temperatures are now rising at the equivalent of five Hiroshima bombs a second.'

subparts.question: What is the antonym of the word ‘fragile’?
options: (i) Brittle
(ii) Robust
(iii) Frangible
(iv) Dainty
subparts.answer: (ii) Robust
subparts.explanation: 'Fragile' means delicate and easily broken or destroyed. 'Robust' means strong, sturdy, and resilient, making it the antonym.

subparts.question: Choose the option that lists the CORRECT statement.
options: (i) Pascal Peduzzi is the Director of UNEP’s Global Renaissance Information Database
(ii) Pascal Peduzzi is the Director of UNO’s Global Resource Information Database
(iii) Pascal Peduzzi is the Manager of UNEP’s Global Resource Information Database
(iv) Pascal Peduzzi is the Director of UNEP’s Global Resource Information Database
subparts.answer: (iv) Pascal Peduzzi is the Director of UNEP’s Global Resource Information Database
subparts.explanation: Paragraph 3 explicitly identifies: 'Pascal Peduzzi, Director of UNEP’s Global Resource Information Database in Geneva.'

subparts.question: According to the UN experts, what steps can be taken to handle this type of unprecedent disasters?
subparts.answer: According to UN experts, handling such unprecedented disasters requires immediate, coordinated global action, transitioning away from fossil fuels, and investing in tech-driven early warning systems.
subparts.explanation: Directly stated in paragraph 5: '...immediate, coordinated global action, including transitioning away from fossil fuels and investing in tech-driven early warning systems.'

subparts.question: Who said that “our planet is burning”?
subparts.answer: United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said that "our planet is burning."
subparts.explanation: Direct quote from Paragraph 2: '...“Our planet is burning,” says United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres.'

subparts.question: Which word in the passage 6 means the same as “original”?
subparts.answer: Indigenous (or Traditional)
subparts.explanation: Paragraph 6 mentions 'traditional Indigenous land management techniques'. 'Indigenous' means originating or occurring naturally in a particular place; native or original.

subparts.question: What had forced conservationists to rethink about long-term biodiversity preservation strategies?
subparts.answer: The destruction of critical habitats, which pushed fragile ecosystems to the brink of collapse, forced conservationists to rethink long-term biodiversity preservation strategies.
subparts.explanation: Stated in paragraph 6: 'Furthermore, the destruction of critical habitats has pushed fragile ecosystems to the brink, forcing conservationists to rethink long-term biodiversity preservation strategies.'

subparts.question: How do we analyse wildlife’s (wildfire's) data?
subparts.answer: Wildfire data is analysed by month, type of land cover, protected area, province, and nation using satellite-based data assembled via UNEP's World Environment Situation Room to produce information products.
subparts.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains: 'We analyse the wildfires’ data by month, type of land cover, protected area, province and nation to produce information products.'

sections.section_name: Section B — Grammar and Creative Writing Skills (30 Marks)

questions.title: Grammar (15 Marks — Attempt Any 15 of 18)
questions.instruction: Attempt any 15 of the given 18 questions (1 mark each). Full solutions for all 18 items are provided below.

items.question: Proper budgeting can help business avoid the risk of ....................................... (bankrupt) (Fill in the blanks with the correct suffix form of the root word in the bracket)
items.answer: bankruptcy
items.explanation: The noun form of the adjective/verb 'bankrupt' formed by adding the suffix '-cy' is 'bankruptcy' (the preposition 'of' governs a noun).

items.question:
Which of the following words in bold are non-finite verb?
Cycling and dancing are her hobbies and she spends a lot of time to them whenever she finds them.
items.answer: Cycling and dancing (Gerunds / Non-finite verbs)
items.explanation: 'Cycling' and 'dancing' are gerunds (-ing forms used as nouns functioning as subjects of 'are'). They do not show tense or agree with a subject person/number, making them non-finite verbs.

items.question:
Identify what type of Determiner the word in bold is:
All the students will be attending tomorrow’s assembly.
A) Demonstrative B) Possessive C) Quantifier D) Article
options: A) Demonstrative
B) Possessive
C) Quantifier
D) Article
items.answer: C) Quantifier
items.explanation: 'All' specifies an indefinite quantity or total amount of a group, classifying it as a Quantifier / Quantitative Determiner.

items.question: He invited his friends to the party. (Identify the verb and state whether the verb is Transitive or Intransitive)
items.answer: Verb: 'invited' — Transitive Verb
items.explanation: The verb is 'invited'. It has a direct object ('his friends') that receives the action of inviting (He invited whom? -> his friends). Therefore, it is a Transitive verb.

items.question: Ritu was declared the ....................................... (brilliant) student of the college (Fill in the blanks with the correct degree of Adjective)
items.answer: most brilliant
items.explanation: The definite article 'the' precedes a comparison among all students of the college, requiring the Superlative degree: 'most brilliant'.

items.question:
Choose the correct feminine gender for the masculine gender- Jack (Donkey)
(a) Jill (b) Nanny (c) Jenny (d) Ewe
options: (a) Jill
(b) Nanny
(c) Jenny
(d) Ewe
items.answer: (c) Jenny
items.explanation: A male donkey is called a Jack (or Jackass); a female donkey is called a Jenny. (Nanny = female goat; Ewe = female sheep).

items.question:
Choose the sentence where Relative Pronoun has been used incorrectly.
a) The idea that everyone likes will be implemented.
b) The work that I was supposed to do was already done.
c) The horse that won the race was mine.
d) The man that come to see you was very good-looking.
options: a) The idea that everyone likes will be implemented.
b) The work that I was supposed to do was already done.
c) The horse that won the race was mine.
d) The man that come to see you was very good-looking.
items.answer: d) The man that come to see you was very good-looking.
items.explanation: Sentence (d) is grammatically incorrect: for people, 'who' is preferred ('The man who came...'), and the verb tense concord is also broken ('come' instead of past tense 'came').

items.question:
Select the option that contains correct Passive Voice of the sentence below.
The children have completed the homework.
a) The homework has been completed by the children.
b) The homework will be completed.
c) The children have done the home work.
d) The children will be doing the home work.
options: a) The homework has been completed by the children.
b) The homework will be completed.
c) The children have done the home work.
d) The children will be doing the home work.
items.answer: a) The homework has been completed by the children.
items.explanation: Present Perfect Active ('have completed') transforms into Present Perfect Passive: object ('The homework') + 'has been' + past participle ('completed') + 'by the children'.

items.question: They were lucky enough to spot an oasis in the desert. (Write the plural form of ‘Oasis’)
items.answer: Oases
items.explanation: 'Oasis' is a Greek-derived noun ending in '-is'. Its plural form changes '-is' to '-es', pronounced /oʊˈeɪsiːz/: 'oases'.

items.question: Write two different meanings of the given Homonym—"Match"
items.answer:
1. Match (noun): A sporting contest or game between two teams or individuals (e.g., 'We won the cricket match.').
2. Match (noun): A short, thin stick of wood or cardboard tipped with a chemical substance used to light a fire (e.g., 'He struck a match to light the candle.').
[Alternative meaning: Match (verb) — to equal or correspond with something].
items.explanation: Homonyms are words that have the same spelling and pronunciation but different meanings.

items.question: Chapatis are made of wheat ....................................... (Fill in the blanks with correct Homophone)
items.answer: flour
items.explanation: 'Flour' is ground grain/wheat used for baking and making chapatis. Its homophone 'flower' refers to the blossom of a plant.

items.question:
Identify the Modal in the given sentence and state its function.
You should see a doctor if you are feeling unwell.
| Modal | Function |
items.answer: Modal: should | Function: Giving advice / recommendation / suggestion
items.explanation: 'Should' is used to express advice, counsel, or a sensible recommendation to someone.

items.question: I saw a sun rising over the mountains. (Rewrite the sentence correctly using suitable Article.)
items.answer: I saw the sun rising over the mountains.
items.explanation: The sun is a unique celestial body (one of a kind in our solar system); unique natural objects take the definite article 'the', not the indefinite article 'a'.

items.question: He is afraid of that ....................... of bees which was buzzing around the ....................... of flowers. (Fill in the blanks with suitable Collective noun)
items.answer: swarm, bouquet (or bunch)
items.explanation: The collective noun for bees is 'swarm' ('swarm of bees'). The collective noun for flowers is 'bouquet' or 'bunch' ('bouquet / bunch of flowers').

items.question:
Identify the error in the given sentence and correct it.
The worker said the new wall panels are not flammable for safety.
| Error | Correction |
items.answer:
Error: flammable | Correction: inflammable / non-flammable (or fire-resistant)
[Grammar Note: 'Flammable' and 'inflammable' both mean easily catching fire; to mean safe from fire, the word is 'non-flammable'. Alternatively, if the error is 'not flammable', the correction is 'non-flammable'].
items.explanation: 'Flammable' means easily set on fire. To indicate safety against fire, materials are 'non-flammable' or 'fireproof'.

items.question: Identify the non-finite verb from the given sentence- He went to the market to buy fruits.
items.answer: to buy (Infinitive)
items.explanation: 'Went' is the finite verb (past tense agreeing with 'He'). 'To buy' is a 'to-infinitive', which is a non-finite verb.

items.question: Rewrite the given sentence in Passive Voice – He will deliver the parcel.
items.answer: The parcel will be delivered by him.
items.explanation: Simple Future Active ('will deliver') -> Simple Future Passive: object ('The parcel') + 'will be' + V3 ('delivered') + 'by him'.

items.question: ....................................... (whose/whom/who) idea was it to go hiking? (Fill in the blanks with suitable Determiner)
items.answer: Whose
items.explanation: 'Whose' is an interrogative possessive determiner modifying the noun 'idea' to ask about possession or authorship.

items.question: You are Saurabh/ Swati, write a letter to your friend telling him/her about a prize you won in a school Science exhibition. (5M)
items.answer:
B-14, Shivalik Residency,
Waghawadi Road, Bhavnagar.
07 October 2026

Dear Rohan,

I hope this letter finds you in high spirits and good health. I am bursting with excitement to share some wonderful news with you!

Last Saturday, our school organized its Annual Inter-House Science Exhibition. My partner and I designed a working model of a 'Smart Solar Irrigation and Rainwater Harvesting System' that automatically pumps stored water to crops using soil moisture sensors. To our absolute surprise and joy, the judges awarded our project the First Prize in the Senior Category!

Receiving the trophy and certificate on stage from our Principal was one of the proudest moments of my life. The judges particularly appreciated the eco-friendly materials and real-world viability of our design.

I really missed you at the event. Do write back and share your news too. Convey my warm regards to uncle and aunty.

Yours affectionately,
Saurabh / Swati
items.explanation:
Marking Rubric (5M):
• Format (1M): Sender's address, date, salutation, subscription.
• Content (2M): Details of the science exhibition, model description, award won, feelings.
• Expression & Fluency (2M): Grammatical accuracy, vocabulary, paragraph structure, word limit (100-120 words).

items.question:
Write a paragraph on "The value of Reading Books" in about 120 words using the hints given below. (5M)
Hints: Books are best friends — treasury of knowledge — improve vocabulary and communication — stimulate imagination — reduce stress — teach moral values — open doors to different cultures.
items.answer:
**The Value of Reading Books**

Books are truly a person's best and most steadfast friends. They never demand anything in return, yet they endlessly bestow treasures of wisdom, knowledge, and joy upon us. Reading regularly expands our horizons and opens gateway doors to diverse cultures, eras, and philosophies. It enriches our vocabulary, sharpens linguistic skills, and enhances communication, enabling us to express our thoughts with greater clarity and eloquence. Furthermore, delving into a gripping book stimulates creative imagination, fosters analytical thinking, and offers a peaceful refuge that soothes stress and relaxes the mind. By illustrating the lives, struggles, and triumphs of inspiring figures, good books cultivate empathy, integrity, and sound moral values. In our fast-paced modern world, cultivating the sacred habit of reading remains the greatest investment one can make in self-growth and lifelong learning.
items.explanation:
Marking Rubric (5M):
• Title & Opening sentence (1M): Engaging hook.
• Content Coverage (2M): Incorporation of provided hints (vocabulary, imagination, stress relief, knowledge).
• Language & Coherence (2M): Smooth transitions, varied sentence structure, correct grammar.

items.question:
Attempt any one of the following: (1x5= 5M)

Option A) Summarize the given paragraph on 'Food Waste'.
[Text: Wasting food takes an environmental toil as well. Producing the food that no one eats squanders the water, fertilizers, pesticides, seeds, fuel and land needed to grow it...]

OR

Option B) Short Story Writing with given hints:
[God’s promise to a disciple to visit her............ disciple cleans her house and waits for God.............. poor old lady knocks her door ............. disciple doesn’t help her ............. tells her not to waste her time ............. next, beggar comes at her door step she doesn’t entertain him either ............. Finally a child knocks her door ............. she sends him away too ............. dreams of God that night ............. God tells him that he had come thrice at her door step, but she didn’t bother ............. lady disappointed ............. moral.]

option_a_summary.title: Model Summary: The Environmental Crisis of Food Waste
option_a_summary.text: Wasting food exacts a colossal environmental toll, squandering vast quantities of water, energy, fuel, and agricultural land. If considered a country, global food waste would be the third-largest producer of greenhouse gases behind China and the United States. Recognizing this urgent crisis, schools, grocery chains, and restaurants are actively reducing waste by optimizing portion sizes, serving strategies, and donating surplus food to charities. Simultaneously, governments are introducing strict legislation prohibiting supermarkets from discarding unsold produce, while households are adopting prudent meal planning and composting. Ultimately, tackling this global emergency requires coordinated collective action and sustainable everyday consumer habits.
option_a_summary.explanation: Summary guidelines: Captures central idea (environmental impact), key data points (water/oil/greenhouse footprint), mitigation steps (schools, businesses, governments, homes), and call to action within ~100 words in student's own words.

option_b_story.title: The Divine Visitor in Disguise
option_b_story.text:
Devotee Meera was overjoyed when the Lord appeared in her prayer and promised to visit her home in person that evening. Eager to welcome the divine guest, she swept every corner, decorated the altar with fresh marigolds, and prepared exquisite sweets.

Soon, an old, frail woman knocked at her door asking for a glass of water. Annoyed, Meera snapped, "Go away! Do not waste my time; I am awaiting God!" A little later, a shivering beggar arrived pleading for food. Blinded by pride, Meera shooed him away rudely. Towards twilight, a tearful, lost child tapped at her door seeking comfort, but she slammed the door shut again.

Night fell, and the Lord did not arrive. Heartbroken, Meera wept herself to sleep. That night, God appeared in her dream. Sobbing, she asked, "Lord, why did You break Your promise?" The Lord smiled gently and replied, "I came to your doorstep three times — as the thirsty old lady, the hungry beggar, and the crying child. But in your blindness, you turned Me away each time."

Meera woke up in deep remorse, realizing that serving suffering humanity is the only true way to worship God.

**Moral:** Service to mankind is service to God. True devotion lies in kindness to the poor and needy, not in empty rituals.
option_b_story.explanation:
Marking Rubric (5M):
• Title & Moral (1M): Engaging title and clear moral statement.
• Plot & Flow (2M): Covers all three visitors, dream sequence, and realization.
• Language & Expression (2M): Vivid narrative, dialogue, past tense consistency.

questions.title: Prose Extract: The Narayanpur Incident
questions.extract: In a little while, the nine o’ clock siren went off. Babu thought for the first time that day of the war being fought all over the world. And suddenly, coming out of his reverie, he tensed. A man on a bike. Yes, he was getting off. Babu flung himself inside. Manju turned a startled face to him.

subparts.question: What work was given to Babu?
subparts.answer: Babu was given the duty to stand guard outside the house and keep a strict watch for any suspicious person or the police, while his elder brother Mohan and friends secretly operated the cyclostyling machine inside.
subparts.explanation: From 'The Narayanpur Incident'. Babu was posted outside to alert the family if police approached.

subparts.question: Who did Babu see that caused him to suddenly tense up?
subparts.answer: Babu saw a man on a bicycle riding towards their house and getting off, which made him fear that a policeman or spy had arrived.
subparts.explanation: As stated in the extract: 'A man on a bike. Yes, he was getting off. Babu flung himself inside.'

subparts.question:
The meaning of the word ‘reverie’ is ________________________.
(a) Being aware (b) Being certain (c) being deep in thought (d) Being Conscious
options: (a) Being aware
(b) Being certain
(c) being deep in thought
(d) Being Conscious
subparts.answer: (c) being deep in thought
subparts.explanation: 'Reverie' means a state of being pleasantly lost in one's thoughts; a daydream.

subparts.question: Why was Manju surprised?
subparts.answer: Manju was startled and surprised because Babu suddenly came rushing and flung himself into the room in a state of tense panic.
subparts.explanation: Directly inferred from Babu's abrupt, dramatic entry into the room.

questions.title: Poem Extract: Florence Nightingale (Emma Lazarus)

subparts.question: What is the prevailing atmosphere of the room before the woman’s influence is felt?
options: i) Joyful and celebration-filled
ii) Quiet and peaceful
iii) Painful and sorrowful
iv) Chaotic and noisy
subparts.answer: iii) Painful and sorrowful
subparts.explanation: The stanza opens with: 'Her presence in the room / Of agony and gloom', indicating an atmosphere steeped in intense pain, suffering, and sorrow.

subparts.question: Find a word in the stanza that means "disrespectful."
subparts.answer: profane
subparts.explanation: In line 3, 'no coarse words profane' uses 'profane', which means showing contempt or disrespect towards sacred things; irreverent or disrespectful.

subparts.question: What is the only thing people do or say when the woman is in the room?
subparts.answer: The only thing heard is prayer; all other words are hushed in deep reverence and prayer.
subparts.explanation: Line 5 states: 'All words hushed save prayer'.

subparts.question:
Assertion (A): The woman's presence brings a sense of peace and solemnity to the room.
Reason (R): Everyone becomes silent except for prayers because she appears like God’s angel mourning over human suffering.
a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
b) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
c) A is true, but R is false.
d) A is false, but R is true.
options: a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
b) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
c) A is true, but R is false.
d) A is false, but R is true.
subparts.answer: a) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
subparts.explanation: Her presence directly hushes pain and profane speech into solemn prayer because her angelic, compassionate demeanor inspires sacred awe and comfort in the suffering wounded soldiers.

questions.title: Short Answer Questions (14 Marks — Any 7 of 8, 2 Marks Each)
questions.instruction: Answer the following questions in 30-40 words each (any 7 of 8). Complete answers for all 8 questions are provided below.

items.question: What happens when the monsoon arrives? (The Flower School)
items.answer: When the monsoon arrives, moist east winds march over the heath, blowing their bagpipes among the bamboos. Crowds of flowers unexpectedly burst out into the open from underground, dancing in frantic joy upon the grass dressed in pink, yellow, and white.
items.explanation: Highlights the poet's vivid imagery of flowers rushing out like school children on vacation.

items.chapter: The Diary of a Space Traveller (Satyajit Ray)
items.question: Bidhushekhar was more than just an ordinary robot. Give two reasons. (The Diary of a Space Traveller)
items.answer: Bidhushekhar was not merely a mechanical automaton because: (1) He exhibited genuine human-like emotions, fear, and curiosity, uttering strange guttural sounds when sensing danger; (2) He showed deep protective loyalty towards Professor Shonku, physically rushing to save him from alien creatures on Mars.
items.explanation: Two distinct points establishing the robot's emotional awareness and protective consciousness.

items.question: Where were the boys when they decided to pull out the watermelon? What were they doing there? (The Taste of Watermelon)
items.answer: The boys were sitting on the porch of the country store on a hot summer evening. They were laughing, talking, and boasting while watching Mr. Wills' fiercely guarded watermelon patch across the road, secretly daring each other to steal the prized giant melon.
items.explanation: Contextualizes the setting (store porch) and the boys' dare.

items.question: There was absolute silence in the room. But some noises reached Swami’s ears. What were they? (A Hero)
items.answer: In the pitch darkness of his father's office room, Swami's terrified ears picked up the ticking of the wall clock, the gentle rustle of tree leaves outside, the snoring sounds of his sleeping family members, and the faint humming of night insects.
items.explanation: Lists the subtle night sounds magnified by Swami's acute fear of ghosts and devils.

items.chapter: The Lake Isle of Innisfree (W. B. Yeats)
items.question: Where is the poet now? How is this place different from where he wants to be? (The Lake Isle of Innisfree)
items.answer: The poet is currently standing on the gray pavements and roadways of a noisy, crowded city (London). This urban setting is dull, unnatural, and hectic, starkly contrasting with the serene, secluded Isle of Innisfree, where he yearns for peace, birdsong, and lapping lake water.
items.explanation: Contrasts the cold city pavement with the idyllic natural sanctuary of Innisfree.

items.chapter: The One who survived: Ada Blackjack
items.question: Why did Ada agree to join the expedition? (The One who survived: Ada Blackjack)
items.answer: Ada agreed to join the perilous Arctic expedition to Wrangel Island because she desperately needed money. As an impoverished single mother, she needed the promised monthly wage of fifty dollars to pay for medical treatment and care for her sickly son, Bennett, who suffered from tuberculosis.
items.explanation: Points out her maternal love and economic hardship.

items.chapter: The Diary of a space traveller (Satyajit Ray)
items.question: What had happened during Professor Shonku’s first attempt to go to space? (The Diary of a space traveller)
items.answer: During his first space flight attempt, Professor Shonku's rocket engine malfunctioned shortly after blast-off due to an inaccurate fuel mixture created by his assistant Prahlada. The rocket failed to achieve escape velocity and crash-landed violently in the riverbed near Giridih.
items.explanation: Recalls the initial crash failure documented in the professor's diary.

items.question: Why doesn’t Florence need a monument of stone? (Florence Nightingale)
items.answer: Florence Nightingale does not require a monument of cold stone or marble because her true memorial is etched forever in the grateful hearts of mankind. Her selfless deeds of mercy and healing live on as a vibrant, enduring spiritual monument far superior to crumbling stone.
items.explanation: Reflects Emma Lazarus' central thesis on true humanitarian legacy versus bronze statues.

questions.title: Long Answer Questions (8 Marks — Any 2 of 3, 4 Marks Each)
questions.instruction: Answer any two of the following in 80-100 words (4 marks each). Complete solutions for all 3 questions are provided below.

items.chapter: Character Comparison: Ada Blackjack vs Professor Shonku
items.question: Whose character do you like the most; “Ada Blackjack” or “Professor Shonku”? Why? Elaborate it. (80-100 words, 4M)
items.answer:
While both characters are extraordinarily inspiring, I admire **Ada Blackjack** the most. 

Unlike Professor Shonku, who is a genius scientist equipped with futuristic inventions, Ada was an ordinary, timid Inupiat woman who possessed neither wilderness survival training nor firearms experience. What makes her heroic is her unconditional motherly love — she accepted the perilous Arctic expedition solely to earn money for her ailing son Bennett. When her male companions vanished and Knight succumbed to scurvy, Ada conquered her deepest fears. Alone on desolate Wrangel Island for months amidst freezing blizzards and prowling polar bears, she taught herself to hunt, chop timber, set traps, and survive against insurmountable odds. Her courage demonstrates the boundless resilience of the human spirit driven by love, making her character deeply touching and unforgettable.
items.explanation:
Structure (4M):
• Clear choice and thesis (1M).
• Contrast between scientific ingenuity vs real-life maternal courage (1M).
• Specific textual evidence of Ada's survival trials (1M).
• Concluding insight on character resilience within word count (1M).

items.chapter: Atlantis: Man's Greed and Nature's Wrath
items.question: The story of Atlantis teaches us that man’s greed can cause unimaginable destruction. Hence we should be mindful of our behaviour. Do you agree? Give examples of the destruction caused by humans. (Atlantis) (80-100 words, 4M)
items.answer:
Yes, I completely agree. The legend of Atlantis serves as an eternal cautionary tale about human hubris. Initially blessed with wisdom, peace, and abundance, the Atlanteans grew arrogant, greedy for power, and morally corrupt, which provoked divine wrath and led to their catastrophic doom beneath the ocean waves.

Modern civilization mirrors this tragic trajectory through unchecked industrial greed. Today, reckless deforestation is devastating biodiversity and displacing wildlife. Relentless burning of fossil fuels has triggered catastrophic global warming, resulting in extreme climate disasters, melting polar ice caps, and submerged coastal ecosystems. Moreover, chemical industrial pollution has choked major river systems and contaminated ocean life with microplastics. Unless humanity tempers greed with environmental mindfulness and sustainable living, we risk meeting the same fate as the lost island of Atlantis.
items.explanation:
Structure (4M):
• Agreement and explanation of the Atlantis legend's moral (1.5M).
• Concrete contemporary examples: deforestation, climate change/polar melt, marine pollution (2M).
• Concluding synthesis on sustainable living (0.5M).

items.chapter: The Narayanpur Incident: Youth Contribution to the Nation
items.question: During the freedom struggle, students were involved in non-violent political activities such as organizing protests and demonstrations to demand the release of the leaders. What actions can students take today to contribute positively to their country? (The Narayanpur Incident) (80-100 words, 4M)
items.answer:
In 'The Narayanpur Incident', young students like Mohan, Babu, and Manju displayed courageous patriotism during the Quit India Movement through disciplined, silent marches and secretly circulating patriotic literature. 

Today, while armed or political struggles are no longer required, students can contribute to the nation in equally profound ways:
1. **Academic Excellence & Innovation:** Studying diligently and developing solutions in science, technology, and healthcare to address national challenges.
2. **Environmental Stewardship:** Spearheading tree-planting drives, conserving water, eliminating single-use plastics, and advocating sustainable living.
3. **Social Responsibility:** Volunteering to teach underprivileged children, fighting fake news on social media, and promoting secular communal harmony.
4. **Civic Consciousness:** Respecting public property, obeying laws, and fostering civic discipline.
By cultivating integrity and active citizenship, modern youth can fulfill the patriotic ideals of our freedom fighters.
items.explanation:
Structure (4M):
• Link to historical student activism in Narayanpur (1M).
• Structured modern contributions: education, environmental care, social service, civic duty (2.5M).
• Effective concluding message (0.5M).
